title: Token shedder failover checklist
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects triage steps, short-term mitigations, and test knobs for the token-level shedder feature (aka "token-shedder") used when hosts experience microbatch-driven memory pressure. The goal is a compact on-call checklist that avoids full-host restarts where possible and gives safe rollback/flail-free options for production.

Context / why this exists:
- Continuous batching and KV-prefetch can amplify per-host working set; when the tail of microbatches grows we see OOMs or OOM-adjacent behavior (OOM Kills, heavy swap, cgroup throttling).
- The token-shedder is a last-line soft-fail mechanism that reduces per-request retained kv/token cache by dropping low-priority tokens from the tail of a request, allowing other in-flight requests to complete.
- Recently observed: shedding triggered late -> deadlock on batch commit path -> host-level stall -> eviction storms on neighbors. Need better detection and graduated mitigations.

Quick triage (first 10 mins):
1) Check primary alerts: SRE-OOM-Host, serving.microbatch.tail-latency>500ms, kv_cache.entries_drop, node.swap_increase.  Note affected host IDs.
2) Query metrics (Grafana panels):
   - host.memory.used_by_serving, host.memory.free, host.cgroup.limit, host.swap.in_use
   - serving.batch.queue_depth, serving.microbatch.tail_latency_p95, serving.inflight.requests_per_tenant
   - kv_cache.size_bytes, kv_cache.entries_active, kv_eviction.rate
3) Look at process logs (journalctl /var/log/serving-runtime.log): search for "Shedder: drop" and "eviction-coordinator" timestamps.
4) Confirm whether sheds were recent and whether they correlate with increased batch tail latency. If sheds are frequent but tail latencies remain high -> shedding is thrashing.

Immediate mitigations (safe to run during production):
A) Enable temporary shedder aggressiveness downshift: increase SHED_PERCENTAGE by +10 (defaults are in runtime dynconfig). Command (dynconfig): curl -X POST $CONTROL_PLANE/dynconfig -d '{"serving.shedder.target_drop_pct": 0.25}'
B) Tighten batch size cap: reduce max_batch_tokens to 75% of current for the failing pool. This reduces tail accumulation but costs throughput.
C) Pin affected tenant(s) to lower priority routing (route policy -> best-effort) to avoid multitenant amplification.
D) If kv-spill is enabled: toggle kv_spill_threshold to 80% to force spill earlier (safer than full eviction).
E) If host memory is critically low and shedding not responding: cordon host from load (mark as draining / no new requests) then let in-flight complete.

When to restart vs when to NOP:
- Restart only when process is unresponsive to SIGHUP and mgr fails to collect pprof or if dmesg shows repeated OOM killer messages tied to process.
- Prefer flow: downshift shedder -> reduce max_batch_tokens -> cordon host -> monitor 10-15m -> if still unhealthy, graceful restart (systemctl restart serving-runtime) with trace logging enabled.

Runbook commands & useful queries:
- List hosts in high-memory pressure (promql): topk(10, host_memory_used_bytes - host_memory_free_bytes)
- Microbatch tail query: histogram_quantile(0.95, rate(serving_microbatch_tail_latency_bucket[1m]))
- Toggle dynconfig (example): curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -X POST $CTRL/dyncfg -d '{"path":"serving.shedder.target_drop_pct","value":"0.25"}'
- Cordon host (k8s examples): kubectl label node <node> maintenance=true && scale down pool for node

Post-incident steps (after recovery):
- Pull pprof heap/profiles from the timeframe (pprof heap, goroutine stacks). Attach to JIRA-SRE-3387.
- Capture a tail of serving-runtime.log and eviction coordinator traces.
- Run local reproducer: synthetic load with variable token length distribution and KV hits targeted to the host pattern. Repo: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tools/token-shedder-repro
- Run experiments to measure shedder hysteresis: 1) aggressive downshift (50% drop) for 30s; 2) gentle downshift (10%) repeated; measure thrash.

Hypotheses to investigate (for follow-up):
- H1: Shedder is engaged too late because the detection window uses batch tail latency instead of queue depth.
- H2: Prefetch + kv_spill interactions cause large transient allocations that are not captured by simple resident set metrics.
- H3: There is a path where a shedder-induced drop leaves stale kv-references that delay GC/cleanup causing deadlock.

Action items (owners and rough ETA):
- Aisha: add guard to shedder commit path to ensure KV refs are nulled before releasing batch (ETA 2w)
- Marco: add a "shedder activity" panel to SRE dashboard and alert on thrash (>3 sheds/min) (ETA 1w)
- Liam: synthetic test harness to reproduce cross-tenant microbatch storms with KV-prefetch (ETA 3w)
- Priya: update on-call runbook with precise dynconfig commands and safe defaults (ETA 4d)

Notes to on-call: be conservative when toggling spill config or eviction thresholds; those changes can cause cross-host cascades. Prefer shedder tuning and batch-cap reductions as first-line options. When in doubt, cordon and drain the host rather than hitting host-level restarts repeatedly.

Slack threads / references:
- #sre-serving-ops thread: thread/CH12345/token-shedder-2024-11-06
- Linked incident: Incident-2024-11-06-mb-surge (JIRA-SRE-3387)

End of checklist. Keep this doc light; move final postmortem details into the incident JIRA and confluence page.
